topics.title: Verb Roots
topics.short: Egyptian verbs are built on roots of two, three or four consonants: sḏm "hear", ḏd "say", nḏm "be sweet".
topics.trouble: Students look for vowels to tell verb forms apart. Forms differ by endings and writing, since vowels are not written.

topics.title: Verb Classes
topics.short: Verbs fall into classes: strong roots (sḏm), third-weak (mrj "love", jrj "do"), doubled (mꜣꜣ "see"), and causatives in s- (sꜥnḫ "make live").
topics.trouble: Students read the final weak consonant of mrj in every form. Third-weak verbs often lose it in writing.

topics.title: Causative Verbs
topics.short: Adding s- to a root makes a causative "make (something) do": ꜥnḫ "live", sꜥnḫ "make live"; mn "remain", smn "make firm".
topics.trouble: Students read the s- as a separate word or a pronoun. It is a prefix that is part of the verb.

topics.title: The Irregular Verbs
topics.short: A few common verbs are irregular: rdj/dj "give", jj/jw "come", jnj "bring", wnn "be, exist".
topics.trouble: Students fail to recognize dj as rdj. The r often drops in writing; both are the verb "give".

topics.title: The Verb Forms at a Glance
topics.short: Middle Egyptian has suffix forms (sḏm=f, sḏm.n=f, sḏm.tw=f), the stative, the infinitive, participles and relative forms, and the imperative.
topics.trouble: Students expect English tenses. Egyptian forms mark aspect and how a clause fits the sentence more than time.

topics.title: Forms of the Infinitive
topics.short: The infinitive is the verb's noun form; third-weak verbs add -t and usually drop the weak j: mrt "to love", jrt "to do"; strong verbs show no ending: sḏm.
topics.trouble: Students read the -t of jrt as the feminine of a noun "doing". It is the infinitive ending of weak verbs.

topics.title: Using the Infinitive
topics.short: The infinitive acts as a noun: as the object of another verb, after prepositions, and in headings and captions.
topics.trouble: Students translate every infinitive as "to X". Captions like "Hunting in the marshes" use it as a noun.

topics.title: Subjects and Objects of the Infinitive
topics.short: A noun or suffix after an infinitive can be its object or subject: rdjt=f "his giving" or "giving it".
topics.trouble: Students always read the suffix as the subject. Context decides; with transitive verbs it is often the object.

topics.title: The sḏm=f
topics.short: The sḏm=f is the verb stem plus a subject: sḏm=f "he hears", sḏm z "the man hears".
topics.trouble: Students take sḏm=f to mean "his hearing". With a suffix on a verb, the suffix is the subject.

topics.title: Noun Subjects and Word Order
topics.short: Word order is verb, subject, object, then adverbs: dj nsw ḥtp "the king gives an offering".
topics.trouble: Students put the subject first, English style. In Egyptian, the verb comes first.

topics.title: What the sḏm=f Means
topics.short: The sḏm=f covers general and present action and, after certain words or in wishes, the future or "may he hear".
topics.trouble: Students give every sḏm=f a present tense. Look at the context: after particles or in offering formulas it is often "may he".

topics.title: The sḏm=f of Weak Verbs
topics.short: Weak and irregular verbs change in the sḏm=f: jr=f "he does", dj=f "he gives", mꜣꜣ=f "he sees".
topics.trouble: Students miss jr=f because the j and r are written with one sign, the eye.

topics.title: rdj with the sḏm=f: "Cause That"
topics.short: rdj "give" followed by a sḏm=f means "cause that, let": rdj=f sḏm=j "he let me hear".
topics.trouble: Students translate rdj here as "give". With a following sḏm=f it means "cause" or "let".

topics.title: The sḏm.n=f
topics.short: Adding .n between the stem and the subject makes the sḏm.n=f: sḏm.n=f "he heard".
topics.trouble: Students read the .n as the preposition n "to". Between verb and subject, it marks the sḏm.n=f.

topics.title: What the sḏm.n=f Means
topics.short: The sḏm.n=f expresses completed action, usually past: rdj.n=f "he gave", or "he has given".
topics.trouble: Students give the sḏm.n=f a future meaning after jr "if". It is completed action: "if he has done".

topics.title: jw sḏm.n=f in Narrative
topics.short: jw sḏm.n=f states a past event as a fact, as in biographies: jw jr.n=j "I did".
topics.trouble: Students read jw as a separate verb "is". With the sḏm.n=f it introduces a statement of what happened.

topics.title: Stative Endings
topics.short: The stative adds endings for its subject: -kj (I), -tj (you), -w or no ending (he), -tj (she), -wjn (we), -tjwnj (you all), -w (they).
topics.trouble: Students confuse the -tj of the stative with the feminine dual -tj. The stative follows its subject; the dual ends a noun.

topics.title: What the Stative Means
topics.short: The stative describes a state: of intransitive verbs, the state reached ("he has come, he is here"); of transitive verbs, a passive state ("it is sealed").
topics.trouble: Students translate a transitive stative as active. jw pr ḫtm "the house is sealed", not "the house sealed".

topics.title: The Stative in Sentences
topics.short: The stative usually follows a noun or pronoun subject, often after jw or mk: mk wj jj.kj "look, I have come".
topics.trouble: Students look for the subject after the stative. The subject comes first; the stative follows like an adjective.

topics.title: The Stative or the sḏm.n=f?
topics.short: Both can point to the past, but the stative describes a state and its subject comes first, while the sḏm.n=f reports an act with the subject after.
topics.trouble: Students treat them as interchangeable. The position of the subject and the endings tell them apart.

topics.title: Active Participles
topics.short: An active participle means "one who does": sḏm "one who hears", ḏd "one who says"; it agrees like an adjective.
topics.trouble: Students read a participle as a finite verb with a missing subject. It is a verbal adjective: "the one who hears".

topics.title: Passive Participles
topics.short: A passive participle means "one who is done to": mrr "one who is loved", rdj "what is given".
topics.trouble: Students make every participle active. Context decides: ḥsj "praised one" is passive.

topics.title: Participles in Phrases
topics.short: Participles agree with the noun they describe, take objects, and can stand alone as nouns: sḏmw "those who hear".
topics.trouble: Students forget agreement: a participle describing a woman takes -t.

topics.title: Relative Forms
topics.short: A relative form is a verb with its own subject that describes a noun: ḫt rdjt.n=f "the thing that he gave" (with -t, agreeing with the feminine ḫt).
topics.trouble: Students read ḫt rdjt.n=f as "the thing; he gave", or drop the -t. The verb describes the noun and agrees with it: "which he gave".

topics.title: The Relative Adjective ntj
topics.short: ntj "who, which" introduces a relative clause: z ntj m pr "the man who is in the house"; jwtj "who is not" is its negative.
topics.trouble: Students make ntj agree with the subject of its clause. It agrees with the noun it describes (ntt, ntjw).

topics.title: The sḏm.tw=f Passive
topics.short: Adding .tw makes a passive: sḏm.tw=f "he is heard"; with a noun, rdj.tw ḥtp "an offering is given".
topics.trouble: Students read .tw as the pronoun "you" (ṯw). Before the subject it marks the passive.

topics.title: Other Ways to Say the Passive
topics.short: The passive sḏm=f, the stative of transitive verbs, and the passive participle all express things done to someone.
topics.trouble: Students look only for .tw. Many passives have no .tw at all.

topics.title: Negation with n
topics.short: n before a verb form negates it, with a twist: n sḏm=f usually means "he did not hear", and n sḏm.n=f "he cannot hear".
topics.trouble: Students expect n sḏm.n=f to be past. The negated forms swap meanings: this is one of Middle Egyptian's surprises.

topics.title: nn, "There Is No"
topics.short: nn before a noun means "there is not": nn mw "there is no water"; nn also negates some sentences and the future.
topics.trouble: Students confuse nn "there is no" with nn "these". Both come first: the demonstrative is followed by n and a noun (nn n rmṯ "these people"), the negative directly by the noun (nn mw "there is no water").

topics.title: The sḏmt=f: "Not Yet" and "Until"
topics.short: The sḏmt=f appears after n and r: n sḏmt=f "he has not yet heard", r sḏmt=f "until he hears".
topics.trouble: Students read the t as the feminine ending. In this form it marks "not yet" or "until".

topics.title: The Negative Verb tm
topics.short: tm "not to be (doing)" negates forms that cannot take n, like infinitives and participles: tm sḏm "not hearing".
topics.trouble: Students skip tm as unknown. It is a helping verb that carries the negation.

topics.title: Do Not!
topics.short: Negative commands use m (the imperative of jmj "not to do"): m sḏm "do not listen".
topics.trouble: Students read this m as the preposition "in". Before a verb at the start of a command, it means "do not".

topics.title: Circumstantial Clauses
topics.short: A clause without an introducing word, after a main clause, often describes circumstances: "when", "while", "as".
topics.trouble: Students translate every clause as a separate sentence. Many describe the circumstances of the one before.

topics.title: Conditions with jr
topics.short: jr "if" introduces a condition, often with the sḏm=f or sḏm.n=f: jr sḏm=k "if you listen".
topics.trouble: Students read jr as the verb "do". At the head of a clause it means "if" or "as for".

topics.title: Purpose and Result
topics.short: Purpose is shown with r + infinitive "in order to" or with a sḏm=f after another verb: "so that he may hear".
topics.trouble: Students read r + infinitive as "toward". With an infinitive it means "in order to".

topics.title: The Pseudoverbal Construction
topics.short: A subject followed by ḥr + infinitive means "is doing" and by r + infinitive "is going to do": jw=f ḥr sḏm "he is hearing".
topics.trouble: Students read ḥr here as "on". With an infinitive it makes a progressive: "is (in the act of) doing".

topics.title: Clauses After Indefinite Nouns
topics.short: After a noun without "the", a plain clause can describe it, with no ntj: z sḏm=f "a man who hears".
topics.trouble: Students look for ntj in every relative clause. After an indefinite noun, Egyptian often uses none.

topics.title: Emphatic Forms: A Debated Idea
topics.short: Some forms put the stress on an adverb ("it was in the house that he heard"); scholars debate how many such forms exist and how to name them.
topics.trouble: Students learn one theory as fact. Grammars differ here; this topic shows the main views and how to translate either way.

topics.title: The Imperative
topics.short: The imperative gives commands, usually the bare stem; jmj "give!" and mj "come!" are irregular.
topics.trouble: Students add a suffix pronoun to commands. The imperative usually has none.

topics.title: Questions
topics.short: jn (or jn jw) asks a yes-no question; question words include zj "who?", jḫ "what?" and tnj "where?".
topics.trouble: Students confuse question jn with jn "by" (the agent). At the head of a sentence, jn asks a question.

topics.title: Particles
topics.short: Small words color a sentence: mk "look", jsṯ "now", ḥꜣ "would that", ḥm "indeed", js "for, as".
topics.trouble: Students try to translate each particle literally. Many are best shown with tone, or left out.

topics.title: jn and the Cleft Sentence
topics.short: jn + noun + participle stresses who did it: jn nsw rdj "it is the king who gives".
topics.trouble: Students read this jn as a question. Before a noun and a participle, it singles out the doer.

topics.title: Reading a Middle Kingdom Stela
topics.short: A stela starts with the offering formula, names the gods, lists the gifts, then names the owner and his titles.
topics.trouble: Students read top to bottom without checking direction. Find which way the signs face before you start.

topics.title: Families on Stelae
topics.short: Stelae list relatives with "his son", "his daughter", "born of" (jr.n, ms.n) and their epithets.
topics.trouble: Students read jr.n NN as "NN made". Here it means "whom NN made" (bore): the mother's name follows.

topics.title: Tomb Autobiographies
topics.short: Officials told their lives in set phrases: "I gave bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked."
topics.trouble: Students read these lines as personal confessions. They are partly ideal statements of a good life.

topics.title: Sinuhe: The Opening
topics.short: The Tale of Sinuhe begins with his titles and the death of King Amenemhat I.
topics.trouble: Students expect the hero's name first. Titles come first, then the name Sinuhe.

topics.title: Sinuhe: The Flight
topics.short: Sinuhe overhears news of the king's death, panics and flees toward the east, a scene told with vivid verbs.
topics.trouble: Students lose track of who is speaking. Mark each first-person suffix =j as Sinuhe.

topics.title: The Eloquent Peasant
topics.short: A peasant robbed on his way to market pleads for justice in fine speeches, which delight the king.
topics.trouble: Students take the peasant's praise of the official at face value. The speeches mix praise, complaint and irony.

topics.title: The Rosetta Stone in Hieroglyphs
topics.short: The hieroglyphic section of the Rosetta Stone names King Ptolemy V with long royal titles in cartouches.
topics.trouble: Students expect classical Middle Egyptian everywhere. The Rosetta text uses later spellings and a few new signs.

topics.title: From Transliteration to Good English
topics.short: A good translation keeps the meaning and the tone, not the word order: jw=j jj.kj becomes "I have come", not "is I come".
topics.trouble: Students translate word for word. Read the whole clause, then say it the way an English speaker would.

topics.title: Using a Sign List
topics.short: Gardiner's sign list sorts signs into lettered groups (A men, B women, G birds, M plants, N sky and earth...) and numbers them.
topics.trouble: Students search the list by what a sign means. It is sorted by what the sign shows: find the right picture group first.

topics.title: Using a Dictionary
topics.short: Middle Egyptian dictionaries list words in transliteration order, ꜣ j y ꜥ w b p f m n r h ḥ ḫ ẖ z s š q k g t ṯ d ḏ.
topics.trouble: Students look up words with their endings, like nfrt or sḏm.n=f. Look up the root or the base word.
